meta.title: AstroSphere – Celestial Coordinate System Simulator
meta.description: An interactive celestial coordinate system simulator: linked celestial sphere and horizon diagram, circumpolar stars, rising and setting, star trails and a review mode.

data.inclTip: Angle between the plane of the celestial equator and the horizon plane = 90° − |φ|.
data.solarTip: Local solar time ≈ hour angle of the Sun + 12h.
data.lonNote: shifts the clock, not the sky's shape
data.lstNote: the part of the sky on the meridian
data.selectedNote: α, δ stay fixed · A, h change with time

info.statusKey: The dot colour matches the zone on the sky:
info.hoursAboveTip: Time above the horizon = 2H₀ / 15, where cos H₀ = −tan φ · tan δ.
info.empty: Click a star in a view to see its coordinates and rising and setting times.
info.raNote: like longitude, but drawn on the sky
info.decNote: like latitude, but drawn on the sky
info.haNote: = LST − α, measured westwards from the meridian

toggleTip.hourCircle0: The half great circle joining the celestial poles through the March equinox point (α = 0h). It turns with the sky, which makes diurnal motion easy to see.
toggleTip.equator: The projection of Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere: all points with δ = 0°.
toggleTip.underside: Show the part of the sky below the horizon (the ground becomes transparent).
toggleTip.zoneNeverRise: Objects that are always below the horizon at this latitude.
toggleTip.zoneRiseSet: Objects that rise and set each day at this latitude.
toggleTip.zoneCircumpolar: Objects that are always above the horizon (circumpolar) at this latitude.
toggleTip.angle: Angle between the plane of the celestial equator and the horizon plane = 90° − |φ|.
toggleTip.poleAltitude: The arc from the horizon up to the celestial pole: its altitude equals the observer's latitude.
toggleTip.poleAxis: The apparent axis of rotation of the sky, parallel to Earth's axis.
toggleTip.equatorPlane: The plane containing the celestial equator, perpendicular to the polar axis.
toggleTip.zenithNadir: Zenith: the point directly overhead. Nadir: the point directly underfoot.
toggleTip.meridian: The great circle through north, the zenith, south and both celestial poles. An object is highest when it crosses the meridian.
toggleTip.verticalCircle: The great circle through the zenith and the selected object; altitude h is measured along it.
toggleTip.horizonOnSphere: The observer's horizon circle, drawn in the celestial sphere view.
toggleTip.altAzGrid: Altitude circles at 30° and 60°, and azimuth lines every 30°.
toggleTip.eqGrid: Declination circles every 30° and hour circles every 2h; they turn with the sky.
toggleTip.catalog: About 1300 of the brightest stars at their true positions (HYG data), with international names for the bright ones.
toggleTip.constellationLines: Lines and IAU names of the 88 constellations.
toggleTip.ecliptic: The apparent yearly path of the Sun, inclined 23.44° to the celestial equator.
toggleTip.galactic: The plane of the Milky Way and the galactic centre (towards Sagittarius).
toggleTip.sun: Place the Sun at its position on the chosen date; the horizon diagram changes colour with day and night.
toggleTip.deepSky: Show 118 galaxies, nebulae and star clusters (the 110 Messier objects and some bright NGC objects) as open rings: pink for galaxies, teal for nebulae, yellow for clusters. Click one for its designations and data.

toggleHint.poleAxis: The axis the whole sky turns about, pointing at the celestial pole.
toggleHint.equator: Divides the sky into northern and southern halves.
toggleHint.hourCircle0: Joins the poles through the March equinox point and turns with the sky.
toggleHint.horizonOnSphere: You can only see the sky above this circle.
toggleHint.zenithNadir: The zenith is overhead, the nadir underfoot.
toggleHint.meridian: Every object is highest as it crosses this circle.
toggleHint.verticalCircle: An object's altitude h is measured along this circle.
toggleHint.altAzGrid: The grid stays fixed to you, so an object's A and h keep changing.
toggleHint.eqGrid: The grid turns with the stars, so a star's α and δ do not change.
toggleHint.poleAltitude: This angle always equals your latitude.
toggleHint.angle: The celestial equator is tilted 90° − |φ| to the horizon.
toggleHint.equatorPlane: Always perpendicular to the polar axis.
toggleHint.underside: Transparent ground: objects carry on below the horizon.
toggleHint.zoneCircumpolar: Objects in this zone never set.
toggleHint.zoneRiseSet: Objects in this zone rise and set every day.
toggleHint.zoneNeverRise: Objects in this zone never rise.

tip.equator: Celestial equator|Points with declination δ = 0°. Tilted 90° − |φ| to the horizon, which it crosses due east and due west.
tip.equatorPlane: Plane of the celestial equator|Perpendicular to the polar axis, through the centre of the celestial sphere.
tip.axis: Celestial polar axis|The sky appears to turn about this axis once per sidereal day (23h 56m 04s).
tip.ncp: North celestial pole|δ = +90°. Its altitude equals the observer's latitude. Polaris lies very close to it.
tip.scp: South celestial pole|δ = −90°. Southern Hemisphere observers see it |φ| above the southern horizon.
tip.zone_circumpolar: Circumpolar zone|Objects here never set: they are always above the horizon.
tip.zone_riseSet: Rising and setting zone|Objects here rise in the east and set in the west each day.
tip.zone_neverRise: Never-rising zone|Objects here are always below the horizon at this latitude.
tip.hourCircle: 0h hour circle|Points with right ascension α = 0h; it turns with the sky.
tip.vernal: March equinox point γ|Intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic; the origin of right ascension (α = 0h).
tip.eqGrid: Equatorial grid|Declination circles every 30° and hour circles every 2h.
tip.ecliptic: Ecliptic|The apparent yearly path of the Sun, inclined ε = 23.44° to the celestial equator.
tip.galactic: Galactic equator|The plane of the Milky Way.
tip.galacticCenter: Galactic Center|Towards the centre of our galaxy, in Sagittarius (l = 0°, b = 0°).
tip.constellationLines: Constellations|The conventional figures of the 88 constellations, labelled with their IAU names.
tip.figure: Constellation|A constellation figure you added. Its stars turn together.
tip.sun: Sun|The Sun's position on the ecliptic on the chosen date.
tip.sunPath: Daily path of the Sun|The Sun's declination circle on the chosen date.
tip.horizon: Horizon|Where the horizon plane meets the celestial sphere; altitude h = 0°.
tip.meridian: Celestial meridian|Passes through north, the zenith, south and the celestial poles. An object makes its upper transit when H = 0.
tip.zenith: Zenith|The point directly above the observer (h = +90°).
tip.nadir: Nadir|The point directly below the observer (h = −90°).
tip.zenithLine: Plumb line|The direction from the observer up to the zenith.
tip.altAzGrid: Horizontal grid|Altitude circles at 30° and 60°, and azimuth lines every 30°.
tip.vertical: Vertical circle|The great circle through the zenith and the selected object.
tip.altitudeArc: Altitude h|The angle from the horizon up to the object, measured along the vertical circle.
tip.azimuthArc: Azimuth A|Measured along the horizon from north through east to the foot of the vertical circle.
tip.poleAltitude: Altitude of the celestial pole|Equal to the observer's latitude |φ|.
tip.trail: Star trail|The diurnal arc swept by the object since the trails were reset.
tip.earth: Earth|At the centre of the celestial sphere, greatly enlarged for visibility.
tip.observerHorizon: Horizon plane|Tangent to Earth at the observer's location.
tip.latitude: Latitude φ|The angle at Earth's centre between the equatorial plane and the observer.
tip.ground: Horizon plane|The ground the observer stands on; it divides the sky into visible and hidden halves.
tip.skyDome: Sky dome|The half of the celestial sphere above the horizon, visible to the observer.

learn.title: Review
learn.intro: Each task has a “Set up simulation” button that prepares the right sky. A correct first answer without a hint scores 2 points; a later correct answer scores 1.
learn.setupTip: Set the location, add stars and turn on the layers this task needs
learn.wrong: Not quite. Try again or read the hint.
learn.stateHint: Carry out the task in the simulation, then press “Check”.

resetConfirm.title: Reset the simulation?
resetConfirm.resets: location, time, display layers, view and selected object. The stars and constellations you added will be removed.
resetConfirm.keeps: your Basic or Full mode and your USACodex and Review progress.

tip.language: Switch the interface to Vietnamese. The page reloads, so the current scene starts over.
tip.mode: Switch between Basic (few controls, easy to learn) and Full (adds the celestial sphere, data bar and review tasks). I'll remember your choice.
tip.learn: Opens short review tasks: each one sets up the sky and then asks you a question. Good for testing yourself after exploring.
tip.present: Enlarges the scene, lines and text for projecting to an audience. Press Esc or click again to leave.
tip.reset: Puts everything back as when you first opened the page: location, time, layers and view. You are asked first, so a misclick is harmless.
tip.install: Installs AstroSphere as an app on your computer or phone. Once installed, the simulation and USACodex work without a network.
tip.pwaReload: Reloads the page to use the newest version of AstroSphere. It is already downloaded, so it works offline too.
tip.sgkGames: Interactive activities that follow a Vietnamese physics textbook. A teacher picks activities for the class to play in turn.
tip.codex: A notebook of concepts: each new thing you meet in the simulation unlocks an entry. The number on the button counts unread new entries.
tip.help: How to use the page, the keyboard shortcuts and the main formulae. The H key opens it too.
tip.about: What this simulator is, who made it and where its star data come from.
tip.viewTabs: Choose a view: the horizon diagram is the sky you see, and the celestial sphere explains why it turns that way.
tip.horizonView: The sky around an observer standing on the horizon plane. Drag to rotate, and click a star to see how high it is and in which direction.
tip.sphereView: The celestial sphere seen from outside: Earth in the middle, every star turning about the polar axis. Drag to rotate, click a star to select it.
tip.firstPerson: Stand where the observer is and look up at the sky as in real life. Click again to step outside.
tip.resetCamera: Returns this view's camera to its starting position, for when you have rotated yourself lost.
tip.infoCard: The card of the selected object: how high it is, in which direction, and whether it rises and sets. Click another star to change it.
tip.infoCollapse: Collapses the card to one line to make room for the sky, or opens it to show all the data.
tip.infoClose: Deselects this object; the card stays empty until you click another star.
tip.infoMore: There is more data below: click to scroll down, or scroll within the card.
tip.term: The ? beside a term opens its explanation in USACodex. Click it when you are not sure what the word means.
tip.dataLat: The latitude φ of where you stand: positive in the north, negative in the south. Almost everything in the sky depends on it.
tip.dataPole: How high the celestial pole is above the horizon. Notice that it always equals your latitude.
tip.dataIncl: The angle between the celestial equator and the horizon, 90° minus latitude. The larger it is, the more steeply stars rise and set.
tip.dataLon: Longitude λ only shifts the clock: at the same latitude the sky looks the same, just earlier or later.
tip.dataLst: Local sidereal time tells which part of the sky is crossing your meridian right now.
tip.dataGst: Sidereal time at Greenwich. Add your longitude (converted to hours) to get your local sidereal time.
tip.dataSolar: Approximate solar time where you stand; it appears only when the Sun is turned on.
tip.dataSelected: The selected object's coordinates in both systems: α and δ stay fixed, while A and h change with time.
tip.simplePlaces: Pick a place on Earth to see the sky from there. Try the North Pole and then the Equator for the clearest contrast.
tip.simpleLat: Drag to change latitude, from 90° S to 90° N. The celestial pole rises or sinks by exactly that much.
tip.simplePlay: Sets the sky turning, or stops it for a closer look. The space bar does the same.
tip.simpleSpeed: Slow: one turn takes 60 seconds; Fast: 15 seconds. Choose Fast to see clearly which stars rise and set.
tip.simpleAxis: Shows the axis the whole sky turns about. The end above the horizon is the celestial pole.
tip.simpleEquator: Shows the celestial equator, the circle dividing the sky into northern and southern halves.
tip.simpleZones: Colours the sky three ways: purple never sets, teal rises and sets, red never rises where you stand.
tip.panelTabs: Four control panels: location, animation, display and stars. On a phone, tap the open tab again to collapse the panel.
tip.latLonInput: Type an exact latitude and longitude, then press Enter. Handy for standing at your own home.
tip.latSlider: Drag to change latitude quickly and watch the celestial pole rise and sink.
tip.worldMap: Click the map to stand anywhere on Earth.
tip.places: Preset places: cities in Vietnam and special sites such as the poles and the equator.
tip.play: Sets the sky turning, or stops it for a closer look. The space bar does the same.
tip.animMode: Choose how time passes: continuously, exactly one sidereal day, or hour by hour.
tip.lstSlider: Drag to wind sidereal time by hand; the sky pauses so you can study each position.
tip.stepHour: Go back an hour, forward an hour, or to the present moment. Handy for comparing the sky before and after.
tip.rate: Changes how fast the sky turns, in seconds per sidereal day. Fewer seconds means faster.
tip.displayGroup: Each group switches one kind of line or zone. Click a heading to open it; the ? beside a row explains the concept.
tip.sunDate: Pick a date to put the Sun where it is in the year. The season buttons jump to the equinoxes and solstices.
tip.catalog: Opens a reference list of galaxies, nebulae, star clusters and comets.
tip.templates: Adds a ready-made constellation with its lines, so you can follow it as it turns.
tip.addStars: Add a few random stars, or enter the α and δ of a star you care about.
tip.realSky: Switches the real catalogue stars and constellation lines on or off.
tip.trails: Star trails draw each star's path. One look at them shows the circles around the celestial pole.
tip.fanpage: Opens the USAC Astronomy Club's Facebook page in a new tab.
tip.email: Send the club feedback or a question by email.
tip.quality: The page has just reduced detail to run more smoothly. Press restore if your device can cope.
tip.resetCancel: Closes this box and keeps everything as it is.
tip.resetConfirm: Resets location, time, display and view and removes added stars. Your mode and progress are kept.
tip.focusData: Opens the full data bar: longitude, sidereal and solar time and the selected object. Collapsed, it still shows φ and the pole altitude so you can see they match.
tip.focusPanels: Opens the panel on the right to change location, time, layers and stars. Collapse it to widen the horizon diagram.
tip.flight: Leave Earth and fly through space: to planets, the Moon, stars and known exoplanets, at their true positions and distances.
tip.infoFly: Fly to the selected object in “Fly Through Space”. From far away you will see that the stars of a constellation are really very far apart.
tip.flightClose: Closes flight mode and returns to the sky seen from Earth. The Esc key does the same.
tip.flightView: Drag to orbit the selected object, scroll to move closer or farther. Click an object for information, double-click to fly there.
tip.flightDest: Choose a destination. The flight is fast when far away and slows as you approach.
tip.flightDestToggle: Opens or collapses the list of destinations.
tip.flightSearch: Type a star's name (for example Sirius or Betelgeuse) to fly there.
tip.flightGo: Fly to the object shown in the information panel.
tip.flightOrbits: Shows or hides the orbits of the planets and the Moon.
tip.flightLines: Shows or hides constellation lines. Fly away from the Sun and they distort, because the stars lie at different distances.
tip.flightForward: Hold to fly forwards. The farther you are from objects, the faster you go.
tip.history: Go back in time and look up as people once did: choose a place, date and time to see the pole star, constellations and Moon of that age.
tip.historyClose: Closes “Ancient Skies” and returns to the simulation. The Esc key does the same.
tip.historyView: Drag to rotate the sky, scroll to move closer or farther. Hover over a star for its name, click for details.
tip.historyPresets: Jump to a historical moment with the place, date and time already set.
tip.historyYear: Type a year and choose BC or AD. Dates before 1582 use the Julian calendar, later ones the Gregorian.
tip.historySlider: Drag to move through the years. The sky changes at once: stars shift and the north celestial pole moves to other stars.
tip.historyDate: Choose the day and month. The app picks the Julian or Gregorian calendar to suit the year.
tip.historyTime: Mean solar time at the observing site. Ancient people had no time zones, so none are used here.
tip.historyStep: Step back or forward by centuries or millennia to see clearly how the sky changes.
tip.historyPlay: Runs time in the chosen way: turning the sky through a day, or passing through centuries. Click again to pause.
tip.historyAnimMode: Choose to turn the sky through one day, or let the years pass century by century.
tip.historyHour: Drag to change the time of day at your chosen place and watch the sky turn.
tip.historyRate: Playback rate: drag right to go faster.
tip.historyTabs: Switch between the panels: time, place, animation, display and readouts.
tip.historyPlaceSync: Takes the location used in the main simulation.
tip.historyPrecession: Untick to compare: the sky then looks as if Earth's axis never changed direction. Precession is why the pole star differs from age to age.
tip.historyMotion: Untick to keep stars where they are today. When ticked, fast movers such as Arcturus shift visibly over thousands of years.
tip.historyDeltaT: Untick to assume Earth always spun as it does now. When ticked, its spin slows over time, so the Moon and planets sit elsewhere.
tip.historyLayers: Switches constellation lines, star names, the ecliptic, the celestial equator and Solar System bodies on or off.
tip.historyDaylight: Normally stars are invisible by day. Tick this to show them in daylight and see the whole sky.
tip.historyPole: The dotted line is the path of the north celestial pole around the ecliptic pole, nearly 26,000 years per loop. The orange dot is the chosen moment.
tip.historyReadout: The figures for this moment: calendar date, pole star of the day, tilt of Earth's axis and phase of the Moon.
tip.historyIntro: Read the introduction again: why the sky changes over the years and how to explore it.
tip.historyMode: Switch between a 3D dome like the main horizon diagram and a flat map looking straight up.
tip.historyCamera: Returns the 3D view to its starting position.
tip.historyFirstPerson: Stand where Usui-chan is and look up as the ancients did. Drag to look around.
